utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Mahindaratne, yesterday I was not fully informed when I said you have to prepare for using less time. As a matter of fact, the half an hour you indicated is still available, within your time estimate. There's even more, I'm not encouraging you to use more, but if you would take 35 minutes that would still, and even 40 minutes is still within your time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, while the witness is coming in may I just inform Court yesterday a document tendered, P765 MFI, and I was not in a position to inform Court the other exhibit which was connected, that is P605, and that is in fact also referred to, in fact the document P765 MFI is referred in Mr. Zdravko Janic' statement that is P552 at paragraph 57, P552.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at it and if it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I also have some checkings yesterday and I can agree with Ms. Mahindaratne so I will have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, under those circumstances P765 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Celic. Mr. Celic, I would like to remind that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Mahindaratne will now continue her examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony yesterday was that at the end of the 26th operation the unit commanders informed you that nothing had happened. Now, my question to you is during the course of that operation before the unit commanders reached the finishing line did they inform you that they had met with resistance and did they request for reinforcement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not request any kind of assistance but I said yesterday that I had reached the finishing line where they were, and it was established there that what had happened had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, during the operation itself they did not request any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I would be grateful if you could confine your response to answer my question simply because I'm running out of time so just address the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, with all due respect that was a multiple question. He answered both questions and one of them was a question that he answered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will just move on without wasting any further time, Mr. President, since there is no objection to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the answer raises for me another question. You said it was established at the finishing line there that what had happened had happened. Could you please tell us what you establish that had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When arriving at the finishing line, it was obvious that a house was on fire. So when arriving at the finishing line, I was in contact with Commander Janic, who also said that he would go to the finishing line. And at that moment I believe that he informed Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic, whoever, I don't know, and he came there together with them, and when arriving at the finishing line I saw that the houses were on fire. Obviously there had been contact. It could be seen by that. Rifle gunshots could be heard and on that road we established that -- that there had been firing contact, that there had been a clash and basically that is where we discussed this, what had happened. After this discussion, Commander Janic talked to me again, talked to the group leaders again, and again we talk with the members of the unit and we established that there had been contact, there had been a conflict, there had been gun-fire so at the moment when I was arriving at the finishing line I saw there was fire, smoke, contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now in your answer earlier you said -- you said: "When arriving at the finishing line, I saw that the houses were on fire. Obviously there had been contact. It could be seen by that." Now, does a house on fire mean to you that you see that there has been contact, fire contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the only thing I said. What was heard were gunshots too. Obviously there had been contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have any reason to assume at that time that the houses on fire were the result of fire contact or have you considered that it could have had other causes as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since the unit was a professional one, at that moment, I could not have thought of any other reason for the houses to be on fire, except for their having had been contact. Furthermore, I have already mentioned during my previous examinations, that we particularly highlighted at the starting line to all concerned how one should behave and we drew their attention to what was allowed and what was not allowed and how the task was -- task was supposed to be carried out. Of course the emphasis was on one's attitude towards civilians, property, things like that. There was absolutely no reason to believe that there hadn't been any contact. That was the only thing that came to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, at the end of operation, were any weapons seized from the rebel forces or left behind by the rebel forces brought in by your unit? Did you see them bringing any weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will do my best to try to remember everything. As far as weapons are concern, there is an reference to automatic weapons because the JNA or rather, our members also had been issued with these weapons. I cannot tell you with any certainty now whether anybody had highlighted that that was the rifle or that that was not the rifle. However, the event itself evolved very quickly. That is to say after I arrived at the finishing line, very soon after that, Mr. Janic came and after that we had a meeting straight away so I cannot say with any certainty whether there had been such weapons or not. However, the members of the units had these same weapons, so I cannot say to you with any certainty well that's -- that somebody said well, that's the rifle. That were zoljas too and whatever else and I cannot say with any certainty what it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, generally when weapons are seized in the course of an operation, weapons belonging to the enemy forces, there is a formal procedure of logging that information, isn't it, a record of this number of weapons seized from such-and-such a place. Now, to your knowledge, and please -- and don't guess, to your knowledge, do you know if that day, on the 26th a record was made of weapons seized in the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you had the report I wrote on that day. It is exactly stated there what weapon was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not asking about your report. I'm asking if you are aware that if in fact any weapons were seized in the course of that operation, whether there was a logging procedure where the weapons are brought in, a report is made, whether this is an logging procedure. Now, in fact in your testimony you said that the weapons are seized, it is probably recorded. Now, on that day, on the 26th are you aware of any record being made of weapons seized?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I wanted to tell you about right now. As far as I can remember in that report of mine it is stated exactly what it was. On the basis of my current recollection I think it was a Zolja, a lot of rifle ammunition, an automatic weapon, either one or two, I cannot remember exactly, but this was recorded in my report and it must be written somewhere. It was recorded. That's for sure. What it was that had happened with the weapons. Whether it ended up at the central warehouse of the police or wherever, that, I cannot state with any certainty but my report of the 26th says exactly what it was and now I've tried to remember, in order to be able to tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll call for your report in a minute, Mr. Celic. Just before that, one other question. On the 26th, did you go to the village Ramljane to see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it the way it was. This is what I seem to remember. I came to the starting line during this operation, I was there where the houses were. That is to say the very beginning of the village. Then I went to the finishing point. I did not go through the village since at that time we had that meeting, the one that I told you about. After that, I think that we all went to Gracac together, and after that I think I had that meeting at headquarters so I did not go back to Ramljane. That is to say that I was not at the actual scene at the outskirts of the village, yes, but not at the place where the contact had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at any time when the houses were set on fire, did you go to that village -- did you see these houses on fire. That's what I'm saying. Not before, but at any stage after the houses had been set on fire, did you go there, either on the 26th or thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not go to the village. I didn't go then, I didn't go after that, as far as I can remember or, rather, on the basis of the reports from the group leaders, I think they actually said that during the operation itself as they went through the village some houses had already been set on fire. That is to say before we arrived there some of the houses had already been set on fire. That is what they stated to me, but I was not in the village myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware if Mr. Markac or any other senior officer of the special police sector going to this place to see what had happened for themselves? Did you know if Mr. Markac went, Mr. Sacic, Mr. Turkalj, Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj was not there on that day. Mr. Markac, Mr. Sacic and Mr. Janic were on the road at the very end of our mission, at the end of this village, but I could show you that position on the map, or you can ask Mr. Markac himself. The meeting lasted for about half an hour perhaps even less. After that where they went that is something I are cannot tell you; I don't know. However, I may assume that Chief Janic probably had quite a few questions in relation to what had happened and I would therefore assume that he could have gone to the scene itself, but I cannot claim that with 100 percent certainty. I didn't go, I don't know if somebody did go, but this is it my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any form of inquiry or investigation at the scene to verify, if in fact if this version of the -- the fact that there was resistance was correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to repeat what I've already said. After our conversation on the road, after that, Chief Janic talked to me. He talk to the group leaders. We talked --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking if there was an investigation at the site to verify the accuracy of this version. That is, that was to see if there was evidence of combat activity to that effect. I'm not talking about that somebody told the other. That is my question: Was there an investigation at the site.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been doing my best to try to explain this to you. I can only assume that since Chief Janic had this detailed conversation with me, with the group leaders, with everybody in order to establish what it was that had happened and whether anything could happened to look at this specific event, it is possible that he personally went there. Perhaps he went with some of the group leaders. I don't know about that. I'm only making an assumption. I went to Gracac then. Whether somebody else carried out an investigation, whether the police came there, whether the crime police went there I really don't know because I was not there at the scene myself. However, I can assume since Janic discussed that to quite an extent with me and with other people probably he went out there to see what had happened because I went to Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 1855, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, while that document is being brought up did any of your group leaders inform you exactly how the houses caught fire? I know you have been talking about combat activity. My question is: Did anybody inform you the cause of the fire, what exactly led to the houses catching fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at that time, in view of the terrain, I sub-divided the unit into two groups. There weren't four; there were two. And one of the group leaders said to me that anti-armour weapons were used and probably that is how the houses caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So he said anti-armoured weapons were used and probably that is how the houses were -- houses there caught fire. It is a conclusion, or a guesstimate, because you used the word "probably."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for contact, fire had been opened at them, and they responded by using anti-armour weapons. I assume -- well, it is very hard to set a house on fire by using a mere rifle bullet. But what we used absolutely couldn't have done it. We used just the most normal type of bullets. It is only an anti-armour projectile that could have caused that. I don't see any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, could you please refrain from arguing rather than telling us what you were told, what you observed, because what you told us is that by bullets, you couldn't put the houses on fire so therefore it must have been with anti-armour weapons which is based on a suggestion that it was the use of arms that set the houses on fire, which is not established, and which, as far as I understand, you have not observed; but if I'm wrong, please tell me. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I appreciate you would not have seen this document that is on your screen. And if you could look at the paragraph under paragraph number 1 b there is an reference to the ECMM group observing a big screen of smoke and it says which seemed to raise from Ramljane area and certain areas are given. That is the area in which the special police forces were conducting the operation on 26th, isn't it? We saw the area Kaldrma mentioned in Mr. Markac's report. You can disregard the rest of the report; I'm just asking you to focus on that paragraph b. You're nodding your head. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading it now. I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you is: That area that is indicated is the area in which the special police units conducted the operation on the 26th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And generally when the special police forces conduct mop-up operations are there other forces, such as the HV or the civilian police, present in that area, in the area in which the operation is taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just talk about my own unit. That is to say, that I cannot talk about any kind of relationship with the army. However, I can say that before that, in the operation on the 25th and on the 26th, we did not have any contact with the army. We carried out our tasks independently . We never carried out these assignments with the military, as far as I can remember. That is what I can say to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move this document into evidence please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will object to this, because what is only verified by this witness as it regards to this document that the area which the document is addressing to is probably the area where the mop-up operation in Ramljane has been conducted. But in the very same document, in paragraph 1 b it says that a big screen of smoke which seemed to raise from Ramljane. So I don't see what -- what level of probability this document carries with it. So I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Probability apparently is a matter of weight, isn't it, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I therefore have to understand that your objection is mainly on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On both way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admissibility. Then what exactly is the argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The argument of admissibility is that this very document, the witness saw for the first time today. He isn't the author of the document and he is not aware of the circumstances in which this document has been produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you know that we have two categories so I'm addressing you. That is documents which are introduced through a witness and documents tendered through the bar table. Would you, first of all, Ms. Mahindaratne, the witness couldn't say much about this document. Is it your intention -- or do you find it a document which should be introduced through this witness, or would you also consider to tender it in another way?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It could be tendered in other way we are have the ECMM witnesses coming up, but I just wanted this witness to confirm that, that this is the only reason I brought this document up today and I wanted it to be kept with this particular evidence together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that the timing of it is because the witness testifies about events which at least on the basis of this document could be an event which took place at approximately the same time and at approximately the same place where those who drafted this report observed certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, if it would be tendered in this context and then it would be a document tendered from the bar table, not because the witness can tell us much about the document itself, although he testified about events which could be, at least by the Prosecution, is related to the events the witness testifies about, would you have objections against it to be tendered from the bar table? And if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that circumstances, Your Honour, I will restrain from any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P766 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I call document 3D00-221 [sic], please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, now, are you aware that the group leaders, did they submit written reports on this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware. It was their duty, because it was obviously that there was contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who ordered them to submit written reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the very finishing line, under the orders of Commander Janic, he asked me to do this, and of course, we were all duty-bound to submit the reports. This was regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know when those reports were submitted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But they were requested immediately following the events, so immediately after the operation, or the action, they were requested, and I assume that they were submitted on the same day. Or, in fact, I can say with certainty that it was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have provided revised translations for this document. Mr. Registrar, if could you could just take -- bring down the English translation, if I could see if this is the previous translation. At the top, we would have the ERN -- top of the document. This is the still the draft translation. We have the revised translations. Because draft translations are not quite accurate. This is the reason that I wanted the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did we see on our screen, draft translation or translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We were draft translation on the screens, President, but if we would have checked on e-court the revised translations were uploaded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could give the ERN if that would assist, Mr. Registrar. And that would be 06377796, going up to 7797. We will proceed with the draft translation for the time being, Mr. President. I will see why the revised translations cannot be brought up in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, the draft translation looks quite different from the original, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the reason, Mr. President, that -- because these are translations provided by the Defence. These are documents we got from the Defence. And we obtained the revised translations well ahead of time. And last night, in fact, on e-court I did see the revised translation, and I don't understand why we can't get it up today in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know who up loaded this. Was it the Markac Defence, I take it from the 3D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I see, the original is a two-page handwritten document with at least an author or a name at the bottom of the document, whereas the translation doesn't say anything about -- doesn't give a name at the bottom. So, therefore, from a -- it is not only a matter of translation but even a matter of completeness of what apparently this document brings us. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the documents the Defence is likely decided to be used but the Defence did not use it in the court of the proceeding and we sent for the official translation that document and we didn't receive that translation for the moment. So we simply refrain of usage of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'd like to note a I guess a standing objection to this practice by the Prosecution in the future. The purpose of the Defence disclosing document to the Prosecution is that the Prosecution is not surprised if we use a document in cross-examination and they're able to deal with it in cross. I believe that documents that ultimately are not used by the Defence in cross-examination and then taken by the Prosecution as discovery in -- in the case, actually threatens to violate the rule against self-incrimination and the right against self-incrimination under Article 21. The Prosecution cannot, through the defendant, obtain documents that are intended only to prevent prejudice to the Prosecution, flip it on its head and then use those documents in its case in chief when the Defence decides not to use it and I would suggest to Your Honours that if this continues to be a practice by the Prosecution then I ask that we revisit how we the Defence goes about disclosing documents to the Prosecution prior to cross-examination because I think it is a violation of Article 21. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a highly contested issue, Mr. Misetic, as you are certainly aware. To what extent even having to present a pre-trial brief is against the prohibition of -- against the right not to incriminate yourself. That is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour, but I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a fundamental issue. I think we could agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How to resolve that, where the line is to be drawn is a matter to be considered. So, I do understand your objection against this practice. Ms. Mahindaratne, there is, of course, a fundamental issue involved in this. Whether the -- your conclusion that it violates the rights of the accused is a right conclusion or not is still to be considered. Of course, the Chamber would prefer the parties to find a solution for it; if not, of course finally the fundamental issue, if again raised by the parties, will be determined by the Chamber. I think, for the time being, this is enough. Now, we are dealing with a document at this moment, which is not there in full translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just -- these are documents that the Prosecution has been seeking for years. We have been trying to get these documents and I just wanted to find that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: From the Croatian government. We have sent RFAs and we have not received these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would add, Your Honour, then that the Court is seized of a motion regarding outstanding documents and I would ask Ms. Mahindaratne then to tell us in court which of the RFAs that are subject to the motion currently concerning the Republic of Croatia this document would relight to, if she has in fact been seeking it for years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage I'm not able to identify the exact RFA but certainly at the appropriate time we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the appropriate time be very soon, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will hear from you rather soon. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have the correct translation now up on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the -- okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, now you have been talking about -- you have been referring to your report on this incident. And is this your report that you submitted in relation to this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, who provided you with these details that's included in this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Group leaders who led the groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: All four group leaders or one particular leader?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I must object to the question, because, already, the witness stated that there were two group leaders, not four, so it's kind of a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless that doesn't make the question admissible, Mr. Mikulicic, because if we could not ask any questions to test the reliability of the document, then of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you in total, but this is not the case. That was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're complaining about leading and not because it is contradicting. Ms. Mahindaratne, let me just re-read your question. Yes, it certainly was -- it was leading, to the extent that it suggests that there were four groups and four group leaders, Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Which will have to be established. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, who were the group leaders who reported to you matters which led to you submitting this report? Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were all four group leaders. I assumed that all four of them were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony so far, Mr. Celic, and even yesterday in court was Mr. Drljo's unit was a unit that went through the village Ramljane where the houses on fire, but according to this report, it is not Mr. Drljo's unit that has been gone through but the units of Mr. -- I think you indicate some other areas for Mr. Drljo and you said the first group led by instructor Franjo Drljo and Balunovic covered the axis Kaldrma via Dobrici, and I'm sorry I cannot pronounce the other areas, and it is Mr. Krajina's and Mr. Simic groups that have gone through Ramljane. Now, can you explain to us the discrepancy between your testimony, what you said at the interviews, in Court here, and what is reported here in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that on the finishing line I described exactly who had which axis. When I issue an order to group leaders at the initial position I also indicate which axis they are on and it is their duty to be on that axis and on the finishing line Drljo said, the leader, he said he went along the axis, his group and the Balunovic group, to the point where the contact was. So I can only say what they said. After the finishing line, and this was a question that the Judge also asked, I cannot talk about what I did not see. I can only say what I saw myself or what they reported to me. For me, the truth at that moment was what they reported to me so if the group leader Franjo Drljo said to me that they had gone through that position, passed through it, then I have to believe that that's how it was. In other words, what he wrote in his report which axis he went along, that's what I then wrote in my report. Because I cannot say at that very moment where exactly he went, when it was in the field. After their reports, I know which axis they went along.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm trying to understand your testimony, Mr. Celic, because your testimony is that it was Mr. Drljo's group that went through Ramljane, whereas your report says otherwise, which you now explain, you followed the group -- what the group leaders told you. So are you saying after you submitted this report you found information contrary to what you wrote in your report? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can recall, the question was about the position where those houses were on fire. Whether this was in Ramljane or Cosici hamlet or some other hamlet I cannot tell you at this point in time but I focussed on the very position where those houses were burning and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's not waste time. My question was this: You already testified here in Court that the village in which the houses were on fire was Ramljane. Now, in your -- in the course of your interview with the OTP, which is in evidence, you have clearly said that the -- that you in fact identified to Mr. Markac that the unit that went through Ramljane was Mr. Drljo subsequent to which Mr. Markac had an argument with Mr. Drljo. Now, your report says otherwise and you explained that that is because you obtained this information from the group leaders and you just reported it as they told you. So I'm asking you to explain the difference. Are you saying after you submitted this report you found that in fact Mr. Drljo went into Ramljane, are you saying that this report in fact contains inaccurate information? Is that what you're saying? I'm trying to understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer this question in the following manner. This was a broad line and there were hamlets there. The question was -- the question that Mr. Markac asked of me was with regard to the positions where those houses were burning and at that point I was only able to tell them which axis I had issued or assigned to these various groups, and they reported which axis they kept on. So if it was in Ramljane where the houses were burning then it was there. If it was in some other place, then that is where it was. So I can't tell you exactly precisely at this point whether it was in Ramljane or not. I just went by what the group leaders told me at that point and whether it was the Ramljane village, at this point I can't exactly tell you. What I'm trying to explain is I can only write in the report what was reported to me. In other words, if it was reported to me that these houses were burning in Ramljane hamlet, then that's what I would have written in the report, and if they mentioned that it was in some other place, then that's what I would have written. Whether it was actually at Ramljane or not, I don't know. What I'm just saying is that I wrote exactly what they reported to me. Maybe it was Ramljane indeed or maybe some other hamlet next to it. My reports were exclusively based on the reports of the group leaders, and it is possible that there was some misreported data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just along the lines of what Mr. Misetic said I would just like a standing objection to the use of Defence documents that we had listed for cross-examination purposes being used as Prosecution documents, along the lines of Mr. Misetic's argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see the point. Again, I repeat, that this is a fundamental issue. From what I under -- I don't know whether we had any questions about that. I remember from other cases that when the parties had problems with this issue that the -- the guidance was that not later than by the end of the examination-in-chief, the Defence should provide the Prosecution with a list of exhibits they intended to use during cross-examination so as to give an opportunity for the Prosecution to orient itself and to prepare itself for further examination of the witness. I have to further explore exactly the technical aspects of uploading and opening, making available to other parties the documents. For example, the Chamber has certainly no access to uploaded documents until they are made available, made accessible to the Chamber. I have to further explore the technical aspects of it, Mr. Misetic and Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may, this issue arose first in this case with Mr. Gojanovic. Ms. Mahindaratne had made extensive use in re-direct of documents that I had uploaded but not used, and Mr. Tieger and I had a subsequent conversation on this very topic where no specific agreement was reached. However, I had indicated to Mr. Tieger and I will indicate to the Court that I have resolved that problem by being much more conservative in terms of the number of documents that we actually disclosed to the Prosecution. From the Defence's perspective, in light of Article 21 considerations that we have, if there is a, and I again put it in the Court's hands, but if there's a tension between the document that we might not use being disclosed late to the Prosecution and our initial desire to just give documents to the Prosecution even if we may not ultimately use them, we have decided to be much more conservative in our disclosure to the Prosecution with respect to disclosing only documents that we're concern to use in cross. That's one way we've dealt with the issue. I wanted to note that for the record in case it comes up that we in the future we have to disclose a document late. It is precisely for this reason that we want to avoid disclosing documents that the Prosecution is turning around now and using in its case in chief when we were just trying to be helpful in providing the broadest possible disclosure. We've now cut back on that and are very conservative in what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's another flip side of this, and you know we get an e-mail in advance notifying us of what documents are going to be used as exhibits. utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have the one. It's in the list. in fact I see Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Randunic nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

The question of course arises how parties obtain documents. If Ms. Mahindaratne says that these are the kind of documents we're seeking for years, I'm not saying that we find that on the RFA list, but just for the sake of argument if that would be true, and if these documents are obtained from official archives that might result in a situation in which third parties who are under an obligation to assist the Tribunal in its work which includes to assist the parties in their preparation of trial, that there could be decisive influence of such third parties on what material is available to either Prosecution or Defence. I said that I raise the matter for argument's sake. It could be a worrying thought. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, along that line that is precisely why I ask Ms. Mahindaratne to specifically disclose that and as an officer of the Court I also wanted to let you know in response to that that when the issue and the Court had the hearing with specifically here the Republic of Croatia on these documents, I specifically went through their RFAs to see if we had ever received any document from the Croatian authorities that the Prosecution sought but also did not receive, and as an officer of the Court I can assure you that we did a thorough search and there's not a single document that we were able to obtain that the Prosecution was seeking in its RFAs, and for that reason if there is something with respect to the special police which is something I did not go through, I only looked through the artillery portion of their request, I would ask the Prosecution to produce that because I agree, and I would also add that I would be surprised that given that the Prosecution has been aware of these 3D documents that they're using in court today that this would not have been brought to the attention of the Chamber before, given the nature of the pending motion before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where I earlier said that thinking about these matters, not knowing exactly the factual basis, that could be a worrying thought. utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I call document P606, please.

utterances.text: Mr. Celic, when you were interviewed you used the Lucko Unit war path document, that is the war log or the operation log, extensively in providing details to the investigators. Did you not?

utterances.text: Did you -- do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could go to the English translation, page 10, and B/C/S page 95.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say to you why that is not in the war path document itself. My duty was to write a report and to submit it. The unit commander compiled this war path. I personally did not compile the war path document but I did submit a report on the operation that was carried out. I believe that that was an omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you said three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could just have one minute. I just need to tender two documents. I just forgot that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you provided a statement or you were interviewed by the Croatian Ministry of Interior officials about the Grubori incident on -- in 2001 and 2004, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice. I cannot recall the exact date. Once it was 2001 and the other time it was 2004. In relation to the war path, if you allow me just one more piece of information. You asked me why the 26th was not recorded as an event. Obviously this is an omission. However, here, here, in the third paragraph from the bottom, you have a sentence saying the unit command consisted of assistant commander Josip Celic, Stjepan Zinic, Bozo Krajina, et cetera, et cetera, so I said at that point in time it wasn't Stjepan Zinic and Bozo Krajina who were assistant commanders. They turned into assistant commanders only later. Obviously there was a mistake so I believe that this led to the error in relation to that document so I believe that it is possible to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I call two documents, please, one after the other. 3169, 65 ter number 3169.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Celic, I really have -- don't have any further time. If you could quickly look at this document and confirm if this is indeed a note of your interview with the MUP, Croatian MUP in 2001? And please try to keep whatever you have to say as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the need for timing but to limit the witness's ability to answer the question to the best extent of his own ability I think is extremely unfair.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was simple, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question was whether this is an Official Note which refers to his interview. Let's first hear the answer. If the answer would be no, for example, then your objection would not have -- make any sense, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had already discussions about the document such like is on the screen right now. This is not a statement of the person. This is a note. So maybe the fair question would be whether the witness has ever seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know the answer to that question. This is an official document we have got from Croatia and that's why I asked the witness if this is in fact an accurate note of his interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then of course he should have an opportunity to read it, isn't it, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the minimal fairness requirement. I suggest the following, that, Mr. Celic, there are apparently two Official Notes about interviews and you already testified that you gave interviews. Have you ever any Official Note in which reference was made to your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And I would like to say that I did not enter the archives and I haven't seen this document until now. However, I did carry out this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would suggest that we give the original B/C/S versions to the witness and give him, first of all, an opportunity during the next break to read them, and then we will hear from the witness whether he has any comment on the way in which his interview was put on paper in this Official Note. And, meanwhile, we'll have it marked for identification. That would be an appropriate way of proceeding. I am, at this moment, checking. The one I see, is this one, is four pages in English and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's two pages -- just one page in B/C/S, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've got three pages of the document but -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. You're probably right. I'm sorry. I was looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you see on your screen is always one page. If you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I looked at the top, though, it says one of one. That's why I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. Whatever appears on our screen is always just that one page. If you would click on the original document then you can check how many pages the whole of the document is. I suggest -- any objections against the proposed way of proceeding. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we have a break, I would have one question seeking clarification of some of your answers, Mr. Celic. And since the transcript of yesterday has been replaced by now, I have to find it again. Mr. Celic, you explained yesterday how the group leaders and you were called to -- to write a new report. You remember the report -- reports which were typed out by the secretary and where Mr. Drljo did not appear to write a report. Now, it was -- yes, you said: "Mr. Drljo was called in when we were all in Zagreb." And you even referred, I think, to a conversation with Mr. Drljo. Now, could you tell us, where were you when you were called in to write the report when you were in Zagreb? Were you at your private homes; were you together in barracks? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it was. This is the answer to the first part that you read out. Franjo Drljo that he did not come. It was probably misrecorded. Franjo Drljo did come and he did attend that meeting. He was present but he did not write a report. He did come to the meeting, he was present. As for the date, as far as I can remember, if the order was on the 1st of September it is possible that I was in the unit. It is possible that I had a day off, but that could best be seen -- well, I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I cannot say for sure whether I was at headquarters of the unit or whether I was off. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you came to write this report, possibly on the 1st of September, you said Mr. Drljo was called actually was there. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, he was called to write a report, and he did not write a report, from what I understand. Did you address him; did he give any reasons why he did not want to write a report? Could you further explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not convene the meeting. It was Mr. Turkalj, the commander of the unit, who did. We did not know what the meeting would be. I didn't know, the others didn't know either. Commander Turkalj told all of us to write reports. After his order I did have this report, I went to my office, I took the office, I went to the secretary, so I can say that after that, Drljo did not hand over that report. Whether he talked to the commander one on one, I don't know. Perhaps it would be best if you asked him, because he certainly had to tell him why he did not hand in a report but he left after the meeting, and I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say you didn't see him after that. You never saw him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I mean on that day, at that moment, when we had written the report, after the meeting was over. We all have our respective offices and everyone went to his own office and it was our duty to submit this. I saw him at the meeting and I didn't see him after that but then of course I did see him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever discuss why he did not write a report at that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't talk about that. Since we had this official relationship we did not talk about that. He was duty-bound to tell the commander why he didn't do that, but I think it is best for you to ask the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00. And we'd like to hear from you then, Mr. Celic, on these interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm addressing all Defence counsel but, first of all, you, Mr. Misetic, because you were very explicit in the issue of when the Prosecution sent any RFA to seek the documents, as we've seen them on the screen. Page 2 of an RFA dated the 22nd of November, 2003, the eighth bullet point mentions a category where you apparently thought the documents shown to us by Ms. Mahindaratne would not be covered by that category since you said you reviewed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he could clarify, we do not have a copy of that RFA, I believe, if you're talking about the 2003 RFA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were provided with it during the break. It never came to my mind -- oh, you didn't have it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, we don't and -- now and we still -- we never have had a copy of the RFA and part of the point I wanted to raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unless it was e-mailed, but I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was under the impression it had been given but if there has been a misunderstanding, let me give me copy to Mr. Misetic right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we focus first on that bullet point I identified and I could just read it into the transcript. It's just three lines. The request addresses the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, and among a lot of other documents one of the categories is all "reports on completion of tasks" ([B/C/S spoken]) completed within RH MUP, sector special police headquarters at the forward command post, Gracac, during the period 4th of August, 1995, until its closure. From what I remember, Ms. Mahindaratne, at the top left corner it was always Gracac which was specifically indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think there may be a misunderstanding here, Your Honour. That RFA that you have in front of you now is from 2003 and I have discussed with Ms. Mahindaratne during the break. I forget the number now. It is 546, is not specifically subject to the request for a binding order to the Republic of Croatia and hence has never been appended to that motion because it is not subject to the motion pending before the Chamber. We have had a further discussion and there is a category from what I understand from Ms. Mahindaratne of a document request within -- within the RFA that is subject to the special police documents and subject to the binding order request, and the category of documents requests documents that were submitted to Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic. So again in further consultation with Ms. Mahindaratne during the break the documents themselves on their face that were presented in court today are not addressed to Mr. Sacic or Mr. Markac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let's then try to take matters step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there an obligation even without a Court order to assist the Prosecution if they send a RFA under Rule 29 of the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Even if -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I also just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Article 29 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If they send it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- paragraph 2 says: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance, or, an order issued by a Trial Chamber."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the transcript. If you're asking me whether there is an obligation to assist the Prosecution if they send and RFA under Rule 29, obviously generally the answer is yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By an RFA the Croatian government apparently was requested to send a category of reports as I just read to you which -- but we'll give Ms. Mahindaratne an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which you say was not part of a later application for a binding order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and if I can make two points, Your Honour. One, I just wish to clarify what I stated as an officer of the Court related to the artillery documents that we had reviewed. Obviously I think the Court is probably generally aware that we do not submit requests to the Croatian government concerning the special police and therefore I did not review that portion of their binding order request. The second point is that, as I understand it, and again I have some experience with this, the parties, and I will speak for us, we obviously are in continual discussions with the Croatian government and if in the course of years we drop a subject as no longer being an issue or subject to an ongoing request from us, we narrow down whatever the outstanding issues are between us, we work to resolve them, and that's how issues are resolved. So I understand Your Honours' point. However, I would add that as a practical matter working with from our side the Croatian authorities I know that there is no specific person who is actually continuously analysing documents and reviewing them from RFAs from years back whether, I will speak for the Defence, reviewing our RFAs from years back, they ask us if they've complied, we say yes or no. If it is no, we continue on the search and that's how the process works. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's practical information. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, I just wanted to add that Mr. Kuzmanovic asked if there were other RFAs apart from 546. Yes, there is -- there are two others. In fact, 546 B which was sent in 2004. That was in fact a follow-up RFA asking them because simply because the previous RFA had not been complied with. And then in 2007 we submitted RFA 739 which in fact was subject to the binding order and there we specifically asked for reports that were sent to Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic. Now, Mr. Markac -- there is a report tendered -- submitted by Mr. Markac on this operation, 26th operation which is in evidence so obviously these are reports that are sent to either Mr. Sacic or Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Addressed to or apparently sent to might not be exactly the same, Ms. Mahindaratne. But let's -- let's -- let's not, at this moment, go in further detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Just to point out that I will not go back into that. But before sending 739, our analyst went down to Croatia and did a thorough search in the MUP archives and these reports were never found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then of course raises another issue. This report, at their first appearance look as these are reports that were internally sent to the higher-up level - I keep it as general as possible - which you would expect to finally end in archives. Of course, since what Ms. Mahindaratne tells us, these documents were asked, there was a repeated request, she tells us, same category.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have a copy here if the Bench would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we can -- if there's any need to verify that that you will make it available. Now, apparently these reports were not received by the Prosecution, apart from what follow-up was given to that. Of course, this raises another question, that is how these reports - I don't know whether these were originals. I take it that these were copies - ended up in the hands of whatever Defence team. It appears that Defence team 3 put them on e-court. Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Kuzmanovic, can you inform us on how you obtained possession of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this particular moment, I'm not able to tell you the exact detail how the Defence obtained those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- very general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very general, I could say that when I took the position of the lead counsel in this case from Mr. Saparovic I have been given the old database that Mr. Saparovic had been collecting during his representation of Mr. Markac. So all these documents that were in the database were transferred to me. So I must make an investigation through Mr. Saparovic what is the source of these documents. But in fact, I would like to add that none of these documents were addressed neither to Mr. Sacic or Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm focussing at this moment on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- category 8, bullet point, page 2 of 546, where at least as far as I understand the nature of the documents and the nature of the category of documents that was asked for that they might well fall within that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I -- if I could assist Your Honour. I don't believe that those type of documents that has been produced by the lower level of the -- of the command and as you -- as you address, that these were directed to the upper level. I don't believe that those types of documents were ever archived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not so sure so I will make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Found somewhere on an attic or -- then of course if there were not archived, then to have the whole series there is -- it comes to say the least as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I could remind Your Honours on Mr. Janic testimony where that type of documents has been produced through Mr. Janic who gave us this document and that was his written report which simply after the submitting to the higher level of command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not -- let's not further speculate on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider what further instructions will be given, as far as revealing the source of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would at this time just ask for 546 and 546 B because we don't have those. We do have obviously the 739 which is part of the binding order, but that would probably help us too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just received a note that generally as practice we don't hand over our request for assistance to the Defence and we don't copy the Defence, but the matter is being discussed here in court and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This of course also -- there's an issue there as well, which comes close to the other issue you raised earlier this morning because there is an extensive duty for the Prosecution to disclose but whether that would include RFAs which may reveal the strategical and tactical aspects of the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is -- I find that ironic because this is the exact point I made at the hearing with Croatia, which was they tendered as document purporting to be from the Defense seeking information which they said free to put in the public domain and then their RFAs are of course confidential, which is precisely the inequity that I wanted to avoid and I had argued for the role that these types of things should be kept confidential and covered by Rule 70. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the flip side of that is, you know, we're asked about the documents that supposedly aren't produced and we can't know what category of documents are by providing us with the RFA which we had never received and wasn't directed to us so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the focus is not at this moment on blaming Defence teams on the matter but rather to find a solution in a rather complex procedural situation where both the right not to incriminate yourself plays a part, where a duty to assist all parties in the preparation of their case plays a role. Usually when I say that the Chamber will further consider whether and what instructions to give to the parties or perhaps to invite them to make further submissions on the matter, that is when I find the issue complex enough not to immediately deal with it and give it some more thought. I leave it to that, for the time being. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very practically, Mr. Mikulicic, or Mr. Kuzmanovic, you will be the first Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will be the first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Orie. Just to allow you to plan the day, Judge, I think I am going to be longer than I said yesterday. I anticipate that I will be an hour and a half, two hours, perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent possible, of course, the Chamber would prefer that we could conclude the testimony of this witness today. But, at the same time, I see the importance of the matters raised with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another matter is whether there would be any time during this day where we could perhaps conclude this afternoon. I don't know whether this would cause you major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe that will solve the problem, Your Honour. I will be a little bit shorter than I was expected. So I use, let's say, 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That gives, at least, another expectation. Parties are encouraged to see what they can do to finish in the morning hours, early afternoon hours if, at the same time, I will ask whether there is any possibility to extend the hearing for limited time this afternoon. Let's then use our time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm obliged Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but could we first resolve the subject of the Official Note that the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes. I should have asked the witness. Could you, Mr. Cepic, tell us or give an answer to the two questions, the first, whether the Official Note reflects what you said; and, second, whether what you said, with today's knowledge, reflects what happened and what you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reflects them. The conversations that we had were conducted as it's written here, but it is true that had I had more precise information then, as compared to today, what I said today is more correct. But there are some minor errors, but, generally speaking this reflect what I said then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you point at the minor errors. Could you tell us what these minor errors were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may, could we get that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, I'm looking for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's P772 MFI and P773 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can't have them both on the screen but you know how to manipulate the e-court system. Could you tell us where the -- and we start with P772.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first portion, I think, is not relevant, but in the first paragraph up here where my information is given, and where my official position was given, the commander and assistant commander -- there is no distinction between the two. I could not have said that I was Deputy Commander because that's not what I was then. But I don't think this is really important in this whole context. In -- on the bottom of page 1, it says that no superior officer said either in writing or orally -- I apologise. So at the end of page 1, where this underlined portion is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, at the end -- at the end of page 1, bottom of page 1, at the very end, the underlined portion it says that none of the superiors reported either orally or in writing that there had been any specific information of any Chetnik terrorist groups remaining in this area. In other words, I could say just as I have said here, that there was some -- there was a security assessment that there was such a group. But here it seems as if there hadn't been such a group. At that time, I received an order that -- from my commander that -- to the effect that there may be such a group in the area. So that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, you said "at the time," I take it that you refer to the time that you gave that statement you were not fully informed. What information did you receive since that day when you gave this statement which makes you correct your -- the content of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that no one had informed me either in writing or orally that they had correct information. I recall that I said then that we had a meeting with Commander Janic, so I couldn't have missed that, that there was such a possibility. But here it is stated that no one told me so, which is not true. I did say that I had that meeting and that I was told this and it was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please point at other inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second statement, the short one. Could that be on the screen, P773.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this second Official Note, I don't know if this is a spelling error or not, but in the fourth paragraph it is stated as follows: "He can only add that he was interviewed by ICTY investigators in April 2004." But, in fact, the interviews were not in 2004; they were in 2002 and 2005. So I believe this was a printing error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac. And thank you, Mr. Mikulicic, for reminding me that we first had to do this exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just -- it was marked for identification until this exercise was carried out. May the two documents be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, P772 and P773 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, at the start I would just like to explain the following. You understand, of course, that as Defence counsel for General Markac I am primarily interested in his role with -- in relation to the incidents in Grubori and in the Ramljane area, and, therefore, I will have several questions about this topic. Let us begin with your arrival at the headquarters of the special police in Gracac. Tell us, please, who issued you a specific task to mop up the area of Plavno-Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific assignment was issued by the chief of section for anti-terrorist activities, Mr. Janic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that in the absence of the unit commander -- Lucko Unit commander, you were assigned to be the operative commander of the units on -- in the field.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Because the commander had other roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you talked to Mr. Janic, when he assigned this particular task to you, was Mr. Markac present when you were issued this task?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get any orders, instructions, from Mr. Markac that related to the caring out of this task?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a very strict chain of command, and my superior commander at that time was Zdravko Janic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the mop-up operation was completed, you told us that you submitted the report to Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Janic forwarded or submitted his report to the headquarters -- to the staff -- Chief of Staff, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the name.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On orders from Mr. Janic I addressed my report to the headquarters but I submitted it or I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff in this operation was Mr. Sacic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber, and for the record, Exhibit P560 is Mr. Janic's report on the mopping up operation for the 28th [as interpreted] which was sent to Mr. Zeljko Sacic, the chief of this department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think there is a correction to be made. It's for the 25th, I think it is not 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No. I said 25th, maybe it was due to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I realize it's a -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celic, once the search was completed on the 25th, have you, at any point, informed or discussed the results of the mop-up operation and the events in general with General Markac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th, no; nor did I see him on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the next day, on the 26th of August, 1995, you said that Mr. Janic invite the you to come to the headquarters in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that you saw Mr. Markac -- General Markac, Mr. Sacic, and Mr. Pavlovic in an office or a room there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this office, Mr. Sacic told you that the day before, on the 25th, in other words, during the search of the terrain an incident had occurred. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sacic tell you at this point what kind of incident this was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not. He just said that there was a -- that there had been an incident and that I said that nothing had happened, and he asked me whether I knew anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Markac have any questions in this regard that he addressed to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, when I came into this room, I greeted General Markac and Mr. Pavlovic. We exchanged greetings, and I think he asked me whether I knew why I was summoned there. I think that's all that he asked me. And as for the conversation about the events itself, the incident, this conversation was with Mr. Sacic alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You explained to us that following this, you went to another room, where you were with Mr. Sacic, and this is where the second report was created, is that correct, that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to add something, because in your questioning so far - and perhaps there was an error in interpretation - but the question was whether I had been taken there, but I stress that I had not been taken there, that I went there on my own, with Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding too. So after the second report was drafted, you said that you had left -- you left it with Mr. Sacic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Zagreb, the Lucko Unit commander, Mr. Turkalj, requested, as you described, that you and other group leaders submit their reports. I will now show you a document and ask you whether you have ever seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the registrar, this is 65 ter 03417. Could we please pull it up on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, this is a document which was issued by the commander of the anti-terrorist unit, Mr. Josip Turkalj, on the 20th of September, 1995. It was addressed to the special police sector, to the chief personally, and we said this was Mr. Sacic; correct?
