And this document states that reports are being forwarded, reports by commanders, Mr. Josip Celic and instructors, regarding the mopping of the terrain. And it is also stated that Mr. Drljo did not submit a report. Mr. Celic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure whether I have seen it or not, but everything that is stated therein is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In view of the procedure of submitting documents, was it customary at the time for the commander of the Lucko Unit to be submitted to the head of the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the only possibility. According to the chain of command, he only could submit his reports to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be given an number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is already an exhibit, P567.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sorry. I'm aware of it. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after you carried out this procedure that you described to us in detail, and I don't want to go into it anymore, I'm going to ask you the following. Did you ever talk to Mr. Markac about the incident in the village of Grubori at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the meetings themselves, I can say that I hardly ever saw him. Even when I did see him, we never discussed this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on through time now. From Mr. Turkalj you receive orders to go back to Gracac together with him and Mr. Balunovic in order to go to the scene in Grubori. That's what you wrote, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You went to Grubori and after that -- or before that, you were in Knin as well, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On that day, during your visit to Grubori, or, during your stay in Knin, did you see Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. However, I wish to note that when arriving -- well, we first arrived Gracac. We were supposed to report to Mr. Sacic, I Mr. Balunovic and Commander Turkalj to report to Mr. Sacic. After that, we went to the actual scene and to Knin, but not at any point in time did I see Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements you said that at that point in time when you met up in Knin after Grubori, it became clear to you that the police, and you're referring to the civilian police, had already been made aware of the incident, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, out of all the people who were there, well, there were persons from the army but there were also persons from the civilian police too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on, you know that a police investigation was carried out in relation to the incident in Grubori, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After all, as you said, you yourself were questioned by the police twice with regard to that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That has to do with the documents that I have just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for document 00605, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, this is a document of the head of the department of the crime police, Mr. Sedlar, from the crime police department and the Sibenik-Knin police administration. It was sent towards the end of 2001 to the public prosecutor in Sibenik. Mr. Janic [as interpreted], after you take a brief look at this document, would you agree with me that this document shows that the crime police department in Sibenik was involved in the investigation related to the incident in Grubori and is informing the public prosecutor thereof?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D738 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask that if documents are shown on the screen and not yet replaced by other documents, that they remain on the screen so that we could use the time also to -- to cast another eye on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, I wish to refer to document P624, that was also sent to the public prosecutor in Sibenik, also by the chief of the crime police in relation to the investigation regarding the incident in Grubori. This document has already been admitted into evidence but I'm just referring to it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, in view of the fact that you knew that the crime police was involved in an investigation concerning the incident in Grubori, can you say that this is a generally known fact within the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a known fact that an investigation was under way and no one else could have been involved it but the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was supposed to be my next question, Mr. Janic [as interpreted], so now I'm going to ask you the following. The special police, as an institutional organisation within the Ministry of the Interior, did it have the authority or the logistics to be in charge of crime investigations regarding certain incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We could only establish facts on the ground. But as for investigations the special police was never involved in that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A hypothetical question but based on your experience, if a member of the special police would commit a crime, then, obviously, the crime police would carry out the investigation. Isn't that right? As we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When, or if it were established that a member of the special police had indeed committed a crime, then the crime police would inform the top echelons of the special police about that, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then the commander of the mentioned unit would take disciplinary measures towards the said member. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please correct me if I'm wrong. If it is established that a member of the special police committed a crime, then disciplinary proceedings would be carried out against the person within the special police on the basis of the results of the investigation of the crime police investigation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. If it has to do with a less serious disciplinary infraction then we have on the basis of law proceedings within a disciplinary court. However, if it has to it with serious crimes it is taken to a higher instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, within the civilian judiciary of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, this morning there were references to the action or operation in Ramljane. I wish to show you a map that we received from the OTP just in order to have certain things demonstrated. I used a green highlighter to mark the area of Ramljane. So could we please have it on our screens. It has not been uploaded in e-court yet. However, the procedure is under way, in agreement with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we have trouble hearing the speakers because too many microphones are on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map, I'm going to ask you for your assistance, Mr. Celic. When looking at the map we're going to try to define the area where the operation on the 26th of August took place. You see the green highlighted area. It is called Ramljane. Perhaps it's better if you have a look at the map on your left. You will be able to see it better, but please don't touch it. Around this area that was marked as Ramljane, there are the names of different hamlets. Can you see that, Vokovici and others?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Celic, that in actual fact the area of Ramljane is a broader area within which there are a few other hamlets too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen exactly on the basis of this map and that is exactly what I wanted to explain in response to previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You can explain it to us now, if the map has jogged your memory.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we get a certain area to search, well, it is evident here that it is a broad area. At first we reach agreement with the group as to how the search could be carried out in the best possible way. However, in view of the situation on the ground there are changes. The situation itself -- or rather we adjust to the situation. As for the question which group went through which area exactly, I can know the answer to that only once the operation is over when the group leaders can tell me we went through this village or that village or perhaps three groups entered one village, perhaps one group or perhaps half a group, but it is it evident that this entire area is Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Two questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I just find out as to if I could be informed as to who made the markings. Is it done by Defence team or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The red markings were already on the map when I received it from your fine office, Ms. Mahindaratne, and the green markings were made by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to put two questions to you in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The red markings, is this the map which was produced by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For demonstrative purposes only, as I was instructed by the Prosecutor Office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these markings. Certainly it as not as I see, it is not admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is not so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not comparing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We ignore the red markings and we'll focus on the green or yellow ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not referring on the red markings at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if, just for clarification, this map I believe was produced through or was given to us which was a map from Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what was on my mind as well. Ms. Mahindaratne, that he, as a matter of fact used this map to say how he toured the area. Is that -- and that are the markings which might come from one of your own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, Mr. President. I was just wondering what the relevance of the markings were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, just two questions with regard to this particular topic, the configuration of the terrain. In an oral report, or if a -- in a written report if there is general reference to the village of Ramljane, am I right if I say that people actually mean a broader area rather than a very specific position where there are 10, 20, or 15 houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That is precisely what I wanted to explain a few minutes ago, or we're Plavno valley, it is a broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Another question in this regard, Mr. Celic. You said to us that groups were established that were moving within the terrain but then it depended on the configuration of the terrain, this varied. On the basis of your own experience did you have a situation in which individual members of groups could mingle because of the configuration of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They could even all be moving in a single column along a single road if the area is inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm no longer in a position to put questions in relation to this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours have no questions, then we can have it removed from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, now we are dealing with the 26th of August, 1995. You were given a task on the basis of the same principle that was involved in the case of Grubori, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the Trial Chamber is already aware that on that day on the railroad between Zagreb and Split, the freedom train went through Knin. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the reason why we were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document 3D00-1455.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'm going to show you a document. I'm not sure that you've seen it before, but actually it deals with this situation; namely, the fact that the train passed there on the 26th of August, 1995. So this is a document that was issued by the national security office of the Republic of Croatia and, as a matter of fact, the security headquarters. The director Mr. Mile Cuk signed it and in paragraph 1, this is a statement to the effect that the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, would take a car to the railway station in Zagreb and then he'll take a train to Split where he is expected to arrive at 1830 hours. You will agree with me that the question of providing security along this railroad right after the armed conflict was over was a very sensitive issue, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Because there were some groups that were still left over on the terrain, so evidently this has to do with the 23rd of August and that's precisely when we were engaged. However, I wish to say that I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we were to look at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the registry for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I ask myself to what extent there's any dispute about first of all chronology that Mr. Tudjman arrived on the train on the 26th; and second, I don't know how important it is for the Prosecution that this may have caused to choose a certain area for the operations the day before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand your concern, Your Honour, but I'm trying to establish a context of the events in Ramljane, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll hear from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will not testify on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we were to look at page 2, Mr. Celic, in the third paragraph from the bottom, you will see that the anti-terrorist unit of the MUP was given a task to provide security at the most sensitive part of the railroad. Is that the way you remember it too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is precisely what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct then that on the 26th, when you were searching the terrain in the area of Ramljane, you were actually carrying out this task, which is derived from the document that we see on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have already said that in my statements to date. As far as I know, this is what we were supposed to do in relation to the freedom train and this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number Exhibit D739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D739 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in line with the task you had, namely to secure the most sensitive part of the railroad that the train took, once the train had passed, your mission was over, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now just a few questions in relation to the incident in Ramljane that you have discussed rather extensively until now as well. After it became evident that there had been combat contact, you said that Mr. Markac arrived and that he entrusted Mr. Janic to investigate the incident. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, Janic was talking to us, the members of the unit too. I was there as well, and it was obvious that this was his duty, to establish all the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, Mr. Janic did testify before this Trial Chamber and I'm going to put part of his testimony to you and I'm going to ask you whether this corresponds to your own recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to refer to the testimony of Mr. Janic on the 10th of July this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we do have a procedure, agreed procedure where generally on an issue that the witness is questioned, his answer is obtained, and then he is confronted with the previous testimony or statement of another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Mikulicic is certainly aware of that. Of course, not having heard his question, I do not know or not having heard yet to what portion of the evidence of Mr. Janic he wants to refer. I do not know whether he was following that procedure or not, but he is now at least reminded that this was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Janic, the question is -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Celic, was Mr. Janic the person who conveyed to Mr. Markac what it was that had happened in Ramljane on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And I think that he called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On page 6192, line 15, Mr. Janic says: [In English] All the information he had, meaning Mr. Markac, about what happened there was received from me. [Interpretation] So that corresponds to what you remember as well, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because I did not communicate with Mr. Markac. Chief Janic did and that was his duty and that was in accordance with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said to us, Mr. Celic, that Mr. Janic talked to you and to the group leaders, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janic says the following on page 6193, line 23: "[In English] Later on, before departure, or before we went other own separate ways the general trusted with me verifying all this information and to interview the commander of the ATJ Lucko and other commanders in order to verify whether the reports were true. After these interviews, I established that this is exactly what had happened." [Interpretation] Mr. Celic, can you agree with Mr. Janic's interpretation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've already said, Mr. Celic, precisely that as the freedom train passed there, in view of the order issued to the special anti-terrorist group from Lucko, or, actually, that once the train reached Split, your mission was over. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the task on the 26th, Mr. Markac issued an order to your unit to go back to Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Celic. Did you personally or through someone else hear General Mladen Markac ever order or take any action for hushing up the incidents in Grubori and in Ramljane or not to have them investigated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, and all his orders that had to do with our engagement were to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Cayley, are you ready to cross Mr. Celic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley is counsel for Mr. Cermak, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said a moment ago to Mr. Mikulicic that there was a strict chain of command in the Lucko anti-terrorist unit. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that chain of command applied equally going up to your superior, Mr. Janic, as it did going down to your subordinates, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also told us, and you have just told Mr. Mikulicic, that during the operation in Grubori, you were the operational commander on the 25th of August of 1995. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. On the 25th and the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, Prosecution Exhibit 772 could be brought up on the screen. As a general principle, Mr. Celic, in military operations it is important, isn't it, that you maintain communications with your subordinates and with your superiors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go to page 2 of this document. And I believe actually it may be on page 1 of the B/C/S version; I'm sorry about that. The bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read to you in the English version - I can't see it in the B/C/S - but I will read to you from the one, two, three, four, fifth line, this is your -- the note of your interview with the Croatian MUP. "He was in Motorola UHF contact with the unit and the men who stayed with the vehicles. They communicated through the so-called small channel number 37 which is used outside the repeater range." Do you recall stating that in your interview with the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And so on the 25th of August of 1995, you were in communication with the sections on channel 37, with the four sections under your command.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify this. We were in contact, this part, so during the task or assignment itself, we are issued a map, then we are issued a channel on which we're going to maintain communication, because we do not necessarily always use the same channel of communication. This is something that the signals people had to determine which channel was useable and which wasn't. So when I say that they were in communication, we were and we communicated via these -- this radio communication. Whether later on we were in contact or not, I cannot say, but the communications were open. They were on but we did not use them. As this is it a small -- the so-called signal channel it is a short-wave channel. If there was a physical obstacle, a hill, for instance, it is it possible that we did not actually have these communications because I was behind a hill. I was on the small channel with my subordinates. But with my superiors I was on the large channel and I informed them. I tried to be as clear as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you did have communications that day, didn't you, with Ante Jurendic over the radio?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did say. We did use this channel and have communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Ante Jurendic was within Zinic's section, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should check in the report because it is stated clearly there who was in what group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll come do that document in a moment but when you had that communication with this gentleman, Ante Jurendic, he was several thousand metres away from you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say so. I think it was less. We should consult a map. I think it was not that far. I don't think it was kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So between 500 and a thousand metres, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to provide false information, incorrect information, but as I was with a unit at the time, I was parallel to them. It could have been 100 or 200 metres. It is certainly not kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 762, page 13514.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This , Mr. Celic, is your interview with the OTP, your second interview.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. The page reference 13514 seems to be meaningless for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's the 92 ter number that we were talking about yesterday. I can give you another reference. I can give you page 23 of 112, and that is V000-5275.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that I'll ask you a couple of other questions. Now, if a unit encountered any resistance while it was out on operations it had an obligation to communicate that fact to you, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this particular section of the transcript, this is concerning the range of Motorolas and this was in your interview in 2005 where you were asked: "What's the normal range, the maximum range of the Motorolas used by the special police? " And then you see it goes on to say: "That depends on the channel used. A small channel for a signal area is something of about 100 metres. On a bigger channel they can use it for up to a kilometre, depending on the terrain." If you could scroll down, please. And you see there the question's put to you: "Are you saying the maximum is a kilometre?" And you say: "No. I'm saying several kilometres. For instance, now what we are using in the city is a large channel that can be used throughout the city, ten kilometres or more, and in the centre of the unit we are using the small channel which covers about 200 metres." And then you were asked about the channel that you were using on the 25th of August. Now, the Motorola that you had in your possession on the 25th of August, was that on an extended-range channel or a limited-range channel?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to stress that as an operative commander I had two Motorola radio sets. One was on the signal channel, the limited range for short ranges, and the large channel which was an extended range Motorola for a couple of kilometres, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, as a assistant commander within the Lucko Unit on that day, you were responsible for the four section commanders, and they, in turn, you were responsible to you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If any one of those sections captured a prisoner of war, they were obliged to bring that prisoner of war to the finish line. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At the end of an operation, as the operational commander, you were obliged to seek information on what ammunition had been expended by the four sections, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was contact, then they would submit reports what kind of fire was exchanged, how much and so on, what happened. Speaking of the 25th, the reports were quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I ask that question again, because I'm not actually interested in that point at the moment. What I'm asking you specifically: As a junior commander within the special police, at the end of the operation, you were obliged to seek information from your section commanders on the amount of ammunition that had been expended on an operation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've already explained to Mr. Mikulicic that when captured weapons were brought back by any of the units they were to be handed over to you. That's right, isn't it? And you gave the example of Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were any weapons, they would be handed over to me, and then they would be forwarded to the headquarters of the operation, or, I would send a group leader or a member to -- of the unit to take it wherever it was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now talk specifically about the 25th of August of 1995. And I want to start at the beginning of that day, and I want you to think very hard about where you were throughout that day. Now, prior to the start of the operation in the Plavno valley, where were you located? So in the early morning of the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to specify the exact time. So on the 25th of August in the early morning hours it was our duty to come to Gracac because we were arriving from Zagreb. After Gracac together with Commander Janic we went to the Plavno valley. I don't want to misinform you but I assumed that this was between 8.00 and 9.00. I can't be more price but according to the report that was the time, between 9.00 and 9. So in the early morning hours before the operation started, we were there before 9.00. In Plavno valley there was a road. We came out on to this road. Commander Janic assigned us to take positions where our left and right wings were and from this road we set off to carry out the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Celic. Time is short so that is a fine answer but if I can now just move on. Now, you spoke with Mr. Jurendic over the radio. He was a policeman in one of the sections, wasn't he, that advancing through the Plavno valley?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We did have communications, we spoke using the communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And as a result of that communication, you took over two civilians from him and took those back to the vehicles on the road. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Because I issued an order before the beginning of the operation that civilians were to be taken to safety. At that point, this member did not know where to take them, and because I was there, and that's why I know that it was not in kilometres but a couple of hundred metres, so I went there, I said I was coming and I took over these civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that on the afternoon of the 25th of August of 1995 that members of the UN were present in the Plavno valley?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say you can't really say for sure, are you saying that you heard subsequently that members of the UN were in the Plavno valley, that you didn't see them yourself; or are you simply saying you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I did get information that they were there in the immediate vicinity in a school building. As far as the information that I had, they were there on a daily basis assisting civilians with food, medical assistance and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And to get to that school, they would have had to have passed your vehicles that were parked up on the road at the start point for the Plavno valley operation, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to read to you the evidence of one of those UN employees who was present on the 25th of August. This is at page 1064. This is actually a video, Your Honours, that was shown to Mr. Flynn by Ms. Mahindaratne, and I'm just going read sections of it because it is not all relevant. That's why I'm not going to show it, but I will give you the page references. If you could listen, Mr. Celic. This is on page 1064 of the transcript, lines 19 to 21. "There was a huge plume of smoke and so we visited that town in the afternoon and we found that in fact almost every structure in the hillside, in this hillside village was in flames." At line 17 they're talking about visiting the Plavno valley. Over the page to page 1065 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Over the page to page 1065, lines 23 to 25: "These Croatian police vehicles were parked one kilometre away and a local military governor admitted police troops had carried out the military operation in the same village of Grubori." Over the page to 1066, Ms. Mahindaratne asks the question: "Mr. Flynn, was that an accurate record of what you observed in Grubori on the 25th of August? "Yes," came the answer. Now, Mr. Celic, the question I have for you is this: You've heard that evidence that there was a huge plume of smoke over Grubori on the 25th of August. Did you hear that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now. Not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Flynn states that the vehicles, the special police vehicles were a thousand metres away from the site of the burning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also the first time that I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So even though you were with those vehicles and a thousand metres away from the site of this huge plume of smoke, your evidence is that you never saw a thing on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. When we returned to the initial positions, I and Commander Janic drove off to the finishing line in a vehicle. At that point in time, we did not see that. During this task, there was some five to 600 special police members and whose vehicles these were exactly, I can't tell. But I know that while I was there I did not see this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What time did you leave to go to the finishing line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I try to reconstruct, if we started off at 9.00, during the movement, we first ran into these civilians on the left flank, and then I returned and it had already started to rain at that point, and Commander Janic told me then that I didn't need to go back with the unit but that I should go to the finishing line. So we did not start off immediately. It was some half an hour or an hour. I can't tell you exactly, later. But during the time while I was there, I did not see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let take a look at some of the section commanders reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And we could please have Prosecution Exhibit 572.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I'm looking at the clock. We usually have a break now. If we start looking at other reports, perhaps we could first take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. While waiting for that, Mr. Mikulicic, on -- on this map --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I have some difficulties in finding exactly where the railway is. Certainly my eyes are not good enough anymore. If at any point in the future, you could assist me. Because you said it was a certain distance from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to upload the -- the map, because on the record now we have the green marking of the map, but is it -- it's not admitted, it's not tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I had in mind, it was a pure for the demonstrative purposes and we could upload it later on with consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that section because since the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- referred to the green marking, if this case would ever be on appeal or has to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has to be analysed by others, then they might miss the ensuing information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, the document that is in front of you on the screen is the report that was produced by Mr. Balunovic, subsequent to the instruction of the 1st of September of 1995. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could, please, look at the one, two, three, four, fifth paragraph, where it begins: "During the armed clash, my group was deployed ..." If you could just read that paragraph and the next paragraph. No, sorry, just read it to yourself. I'm just trying to save time. If could you just read it, because everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is information that was not dictated to you by Mr. Sacic on the 25th of August -- on the 26th of August of 1995 in the morning, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So by this period, it was absolutely clear to you that Mr. Balunovic did actually know what happened in Grubori on the 25th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he knew and whether he adjusted his report to mine, the one that I had to write as dictated, that is something I don't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you can see here clearly that there is new information that is contained in this report that's not in the information dictated to you by Mr. Sacic, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he was your friend. Did you discuss the matter with him? Did you ask him where he got this information from, whether it was his personal knowledge, or whether somebody else had told him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if somebody else had told him. I assume that he adjusted his report to my report, and that within that, he compiled his report and then he inserted this other section. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In that section, the part that he inserted, I'll ask you the question again: Did you ask him personally whether this was his own information, whether these were facts that he was aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer you quite frankly. Everything I have been saying has been the truth. I don't remember that we discussed that section. But I do know that he had not known of what had happened down there because when we had to travel down there on the second or third day did he not know. Again, so I am convinced that he did not what had happened down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you were his commander, weren't you, during the operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he provided you with information on the 1st of September about the operation which you did not have prior to that date, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, the 1st of September? Actually, I would like to say that his information after the terrain was that nothing had happened and this was written on the 2nd of September on orders from Commander Turkalj. But in relation to myself and Mr. Balunovic, I wish to say that his oral report after the end of the action was also that nothing had happened. This report was written later, and it also describes that something had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just to close this down, because I don't want to go on endlessly on this, but in terms of the information contained in paragraphs 5 and 6 of this report, it's your evidence that you did not ever discuss those matters with Mr. Balunovic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read his report, but I did not specifically single out paragraphs 5 or 6 and ask him why he had written that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ask him any questions about this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day when we had the meeting with our immediate commander we were all duty-bound to attend and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'm going to interrupt you because my time is short. It's a simple question: Did you personally as his operational commander ever ask Mr. Balunovic about the contents of his report that was dated 25th August 1995, the report that is in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll say once again on the day when the reports were written we did talk about. On that day, he also wrote his report on his own. He submitted it to the secretary, but we did not specifically discuss what it was that he had written down there. We did not discuss it in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what Mr. Sacic had told you on the 26th of August of 1995, were you in any way surprised by the additional information in Mr. Balunovic's report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my own report, I said that out of all of the information contained in my report I did not know about all of that. I have already said that. And obviously other reports were adapted to my report. So my report, the information contained in my report was something I didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'll ask you the question once again and then I'm going to move on. Bearing in mind what Mr. Sacic had told you on the 26th of August of 1995, were you in any way surprised or interested by the additional information contained in Mr. Balunovic's report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes. The whole situation was different. The first contact was that it had not happened, and then afterwards, it turned out that something had happened after all, so the situation was quite different from the statements that were made right after the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So though you were surprised and interested, you never directly discussed with Mr. Balunovic this new information contained in his report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I've answered that question for you already. We did talk, and he was convinced then as well that nothing had happened and that he knew nothing. Obviously the report was adapted to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can please look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 569.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can just go to the bottom of that particular page, you see, Mr. Celic, that this is Mr. Zinic's report, and, again, in order to preserve time, if you could look at the large paragraph that is the third from the bottom of the report, which begins: "While I was on the left side of Grubori village there was sudden, fierce gun-fire and several explosions were heard." Could you read that paragraph to yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zinic indicates that he received information about a group of Chetniks over the system. And he's there referring to your radio communication system, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that he also heard very fierce gun-fire and several explosions. You see that too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the 12 men that were under his command, one of them, number 8 is Ante Jurendic who is the individual with whom you had radio communications earlier in the day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the system over which Mr. Zinic heard that there were Chetniks -- heard that another group had come upon a group of Chetniks was the same system on which you were listening, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. However, I wish to point out that I did not hear this conversation over the communications equipment and I did have my communications equipment with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were on the same network at the time, but your evidence is you did not hear what Mr. Zinic heard about Chetniks -- about a group coming upon a group of Chetniks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, if I just -- I just want to point out but in fairness to the Defence I would not want the witness to have the benefit of this -- if it is not translated to the -- interpreted to the witness what I'm going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can't ask the interpreters not to translate something because the whole of the public would be -- what we could ask. Mr. Celic, do you speak any English? Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I understand some words, very little. I don't speak the language though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to say, Ms. Mahindaratne, so I don't know whether it is sufficient, if it is complex enough for someone who knows only a few words not to understand or I've got no idea. So I leave it up to you whether or not we will just ask the witness to take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, could you take the earphones off for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just want to point out that the name that Mr. Cayley just mentioned also transpires in another report of one of the other group leaders. That is P771 and P768. I will not -- I will refrain from using the names so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me, which, of course, still leaves open the question whether these are several persons with the same name or whether this is a person with the skill of being at several places at the same time. Mr. Celic, could you please put your earphones on again. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, just to clarify one thing, we -- Ante Jurendic named in this report by Mr. Zinic is the same Ante Jurendic who you met with the two civilians earlier in the day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move to the night of the 25th of August of 1995. You returned to which location after the operation was finished and the units had come to the finish line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you went with your men, with your four sections back to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on the journey back to Gracac, nobody spoke amongst themselves, like soldiers do, about the operation that had just taken place in the Plavno valley?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether people were talking amongst themselves is something that I would not know today. I can just say that in my vehicle, and there were five people in every vehicle, I was convinced, like the rest, that nothing had happened, absolutely. Whether somebody else was discussing something else in a different vehicle or something, I don't know. However, all the information that I had at that time and that I heard was to the effect that nothing had happened. I cannot assert now whether someone in the fifth or tenth vehicle discussed that. However, I'm talking to you about things that have to do with me. I personally had information that on that day, nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was in your vehicle with you when you returned from the Plavno valley to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't remember now exactly who was there. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it the section commanders? Zinic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just be making a mistake if I said anything. I had a driver and perhaps two or three other members of the unit or perhaps I was on my own with the driver. I really could not say. Whatever I would say would not be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's look at P563, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the operation on the 25th of August, at the finish line, I want you to think about that for a moment, you answered to me earlier that it was standard practice at the end of an operation for you to do a review, do an ammunition check to find out how much ammunition had been expended by the unit. Do you recall that evidence that you said to me earlier today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have already asked me that. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question because I have a specific question for you. When you did the ammunition check, on the Lucko Unit, when it arrived on the finish line on the 25th of August of 1995, did you find ammunition had been expended by the men of the four sections?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the answer is I did not check how much ammunition they had on them. This was due to the fact that there was no reason for me to check that on the basis of the reports of the group leaders. Had anything been done, then the members who had done that would have reported to the leader so I did not line up the unit myself to check. There was no check that day, that is what I'm saying, in view of the report that I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But it was normally standard practice for you on every operation, wasn't it, as you've said earlier, to check how much ammunition had been used?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You misunderstood. It was not customary after an operation ended that ammunition reports were made. After all the tasks had been accomplished, depending on the task, we would check whether everyone was okay, whether there were any losses, whether there were casualties and then they would report it themselves. But absolutely never, not in a single task, would there be a lineup of men and then checking how much ammunition they had or not, especially in view of the fact that after such operations men were tired, exhausted and there was no need to bother them with this additional burden. So if there had been any ammunition expended, the user himself would have reported this to his group leader, and then it would have reached me. But it was not customary to go from one special to -- member of the special police and check with them whether there had been any expenditures of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you ensure on any operation that a special policemen actually did report that he had expended ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a chain of command within any unit itself. So me, as an operational officer, I had group leaders. They were -- they would lead groups of up to ten men and then within that group of men there would be a specialised leader who would have three or four men under himself so there would be three or four commanders -- four or five commanders that would need to relate this information and I wouldn't go from one to the other to check it. As for ammunition itself, I can tell you the following. When weapons and ammunition is issued, it is registered in the card -- the personal file of the user how much ammunition he was issued and it was his responsibility to report any use of ammunition. During the advance of our unit, because Operation Storm lasted a couple of days, there was no special reporting on how much ammunition was exactly issued, whether someone took 50 or 100 rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's look at 563. This is the report that was dictated to you by Mr. Sacic on the morning of the 26th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But the report itself, but you said the 26th on the morning. I wouldn't be as specific. I wouldn't say it was then exactly. I can't give you exact information as to when exactly it was. But is this the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what interests me about this particular report is the following. He told you in this report that an arrested person Stevan Karanovic, around 30 years old, had been brought in by the special police, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you knew, at least from your knowledge, that nobody, that no prisoners of war in fact arrived with the special police at the finish line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this report also refers to two weapons being seized. And you didn't see any seized weapons at the finish line, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, also at the bottom of this report it refers to the village of Grubor being placed under the control of 20 members of the Lucko ATJ under the commander of Franjo Drljo and Bozo Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this report suggesting that those two sections of the special police remained in Grubori whilst the others came to the finish line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these two sections remained there until just prior to 4.00 and then returned with everybody else to the finish line. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How much time they spent where, I can't tell you exactly. But I can tell you that at the finish line, within 15 to 30 minutes, everyone arrived there, more or less. So it's not true that they were someplace else and arrived later. They arrived at the finish line already by 1600 hours, as you can see in this report. Some people may have arrived earlier, others later, but I have to stress that this was a hilly area and they had to come down from a hill. There was a steep incline there, so they arrived in different batches and groups, and they arrived tired and wet and they -- all they were looking for was to get to the vehicles and change as soon as possible. So they didn't all arrive at the same time but they arrived within a period of a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When Mr. Sacic dictated this report to you, you told him that you had not seen any prisoner of war or any captured weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I went to the headquarters where I was with Mr. Sacic, he had my report that nothing had happened and he asked me about the report. I repeated the entire account of where I was during this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I told him that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'm going to interrupt you because my time is running out. The question I have for you is this. When Mr. Sacic dictated this report to you on either the 25th or the 26th of August, did you inform him that you had not seen a prisoner of war and you had not seen any captured weapons, since you were actually signing this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was trying to tell you. So I told him that nothing had happened, that there had been no incident, no prisoner of war, nothing. That's exactly what I told him. But I also told him that this was the information that I got from the group leaders. However, based on what he requested from me, I did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you signed a report where you essentially could not confirm the information that was in it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you must have asked Mr. Sacic where he got his information from, correct, because he was your superior?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him. He told me himself. That obviously there had been a clash there, that there were prisoners of war but all this information that he relayed to me didn't really have any meaning to me then. However, now, I do -- it does have some meaning. But as for the information itself, neither then nor now do they have any relevance to me because I could neither confirm them nor deny them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you were the operational commander during this operation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You had four sections of men under your command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It never crossed your mind when you were speaking with Mr. Sacic to ask him who had told him about what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him to call, to summon the group leaders and ask them. As for who told him of what had happened, I don't know. He was my immediate superior and he was the authority for me, and based on that, I carried out the order that he issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said to us earlier that there was a strict command structure within the Lucko anti-terrorist unit. Did you ask your section commanders who had been speaking to Mr. Sacic about what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask if anybody had spoken with Sacic. At that point in time, on the 26th, I was there alone on my own. There were no group leaders but I asked Mr. Sacic to summon the group leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when this information had been given to you, did it become fairly obvious that there had been a contact in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what he said, there was no reason for me to disbelieve what he said. That became obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated yesterday to this Court when you were talking about the operation on the 26th of August in Ramljane, that the following, I will read it, it on page 8017 to 8018, lines 23 through to line 3 on the next page: "And when the leader of the group in talking to him saw that the General insisted, he said that he passed by that way and that there was fighting." And now we're talking about the 26th of August. "And he was angry in his responses, and I think he mentioned everything, and I know that on the same day, we had to establish the facts because it was obvious, it was evident that there had been contact." Now, the question I have for you is that if Mr. Sacic made it obvious and evident to you that there had been contact in Grubori, why did you not establish the facts of what had happened there, as you were saying in the case of the operation on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I can tell you this: At that moment when I was Mr. Sacic I believe the unit was already on its way to Zagreb. So at that point I had no opportunity to talk -- discuss this with him. A detailed conversation about this event was conducted when we were summoned up by the commander which was two or three days later, and we were all there together. When I returned to Zagreb, in other words, and the men who had -- had -- who had their days off, they weren't there two or three days, so they weren't within the unit, but I believe already on the second day when I returned to Zagreb I had to go back and this is the first time that I went to Grubori and saw what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I said this when you asked me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's stop and go back to the question. Did you not feel as an assistant commander within the Lucko anti-terrorist unit that after Mr. Sacic had told you these facts that had you an obligation to establish what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the written reports submitted to the headquarters, I had reported all of this. My responsibility was to inform the headquarters of anything that happened at -- in the field, not Mr. Sacic, but Mr. Janic. And also, when I returned to the unit it was my duty to explain everything that had happened exactly then. I cannot give you the precise date. I can't say exactly but I think it was the 26th so I was still down there. When I arrived in the unit my commander was there, he was informed of all of the events and then I went together with my commander to the field. My responsibility was to inform the commander of everything that I had done. But I cannot speak of things that I don't know. If a group leader reported something to me, that's how I had to report it on, because I could not say anything else. I can only speak of the facts that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Between the 26th and the 1st -- the 26th of August and the 1st of September, you must have spoken with members of the Lucko anti-terrorist unit, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that I did talk with Mr. Balunovic. The men were on leave on that day because we returned on the 27th, and our next meeting was on the 1st. On those couple of days the men were on leave, and I cannot speak for certain about the time. I know that I spoke with Mr. Balunovic about this, but I don't know if I discussed it with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that what Mr. Sacic had dictated you -- dictated to you was a fairly dramatic and worrying report, did you not feel as a junior commander that you should call these men back from leave and establish the facts of what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reiterate what I've said before. From the point when I had the meeting with Sacic - this was on the 26th, in the afternoon as far as I can ascertain, but I think you can check that exactly - so the day after that I returned to Zagreb and then on the next day I went back there and on that next day I went back to Grubori and I saw what had happened there. So at that point, there was no one could I talk to because the men were on leave because I only went to Zagreb for one day, I spent the night there, and then I returned. I had to be in Gracac the next day already. So there was no one I could discuss this with except Mr. Balunovic, who went back with me, and then I saw that there had been contact there on the axis where we passed, that there was an engagement of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You returned to Zagreb on the 27th of August, didn't you, from Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Please don't hold me exactly on what I'm saying, but I believe it was on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Between the 27th of August and the receipt of the order of the 1st of September to make a report, did you not feel obliged as a junior commander to speak to your four section commanders about what had happened in Grubori on the 25th of August of 1995, bearing in mind what Mr. Sacic had told you on the 25th or 26th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't take my word for it when I mention the date, because I might misinform you. But we did discuss this in this meeting a couple of days later, and I think that at that time - in other words when I returned - the men were on leave and I was on leave. So two or three days later we had the meeting and we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Celic, specifically what did you, because you were a junior commander. Did you not thing bearing in mind what Mr. Sacic told you that it was more important to establish the facts of what happened in Grubori than for the men to be enjoying three days leave in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sacic did not issue any specific instructions to that effect, and I -- it was my duty to submit my report, and did I not get any instructions from him to speak to anyone. I had this information from my immediate superior who also mentioned what had happened, because he was present there, and then we had this meeting where the group leaders, we discussed this, because you mentioned Mr. Balunovic specifically. I can say in his report too it was stated that nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak, I appreciate your efforts I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't think I'm going to finish, Your Honour, but I will certainly move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not going to finish. By when?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I'd probably need about another sort of three quarters of an hour, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no re-examination so far, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No questions from us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from you. In view of all this, I would ask you to see whether you could finish in not more than 30 minutes. We would have until quarter past 2.00. We can have an extended session today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When Mr. Sacic dictated to the report to you of what had taken place in Grubori and that he told you that two women had been killed and two elderly men, did the word "murder" cross your mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained this by the fact that I believed him at the moment when he told me everything. I had no reason not to believe him because he was the chief of sector at the time, and for me he was my immediate superior and he had authority and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Celic, I'm running out of time and I need you to directly address the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- Mr. Celic, in your last answer you said you had no reason not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as you told us in quite some detail that there was no -- you couldn't hear anything that came close to combat activity. You've told us that there were no prisoners of war at the end of the day. Would these two reasons not be good reasons to at least have serious doubt on whether the authority you refer to told you what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as what he said to me is concerned, it would be best if you asked him, but I know that there were no prisoners and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no doubt in my mind because I believed that things were the way he had put it to me. In the report when we wrote about prisoners, he knew about my report and I said that as far as I knew there were no prisoners and that not a single group leader had reported to me stating that there were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are all reasons to doubt his version, isn't it? Whether you believed him or not is another question, but just objectively. If he would have told you -- let me put things quite simple. If he would have told that you the whole operation had taken place during the night, would you have believed him? Whereas your own observation was that it took place during the day, isn't it? Would you, under his authority, have believed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no reason not to believe him. As for the operation itself, if I know where my men are it is only natural that the facts indicate that to me. However, I will answer you now. Although I had information that there were no prisoners I really believed them then that that actually was the case. Obviously there had been some kind of a clash because this is what he had said. Finally when we went there we did see that there had been a clash. However, now, should one believe the group leaders who had told me that nothing had happened. He said that something had happened and that I should write that up and ultimately it was established that something had happened. At that moment I had no reason not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your own observations supported what your group leaders had told you because you didn't hear firing of arms, which would be of the combat type, and there were no prisoners of war at the end of the day. What was told to you by your authority was not consistent with your own observations. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I fully agree with that. However, I would like to try to paint a picture of what the situation was on the ground. Along the line, during -- along this one kilometre I really could not tell whether something had happened. That is to say, that I always left open the possibility that there was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are -- Mr. Cayley, please proceed, and whether are reasons, objective reasons is finally not for the witness to decide. He can tell us whether he believed or did not believe. Whether there are objective reasons on the basis of what he told us to have doubt or no doubt is finally a matter the Chamber, of course, is able to determine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try and finish in the next ten or 15 minutes on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let us move to the 27th of August of 1995. What time did you arrive in Knin for your visit on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. Perhaps around midday, 1.00 or 2.00 but I cannot tell you exactly. Roughly around midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you travelled down from Zagreb with Mr. Balunovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Turkalj travelled separately or with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Separately, in a different car.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk specifically about what you saw in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could have P761. And I will have to find, Mr. Registrar, the correct page for your reference. It's page 13765. And that is page 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The ERN number would be V000-4126.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Celic, I'm right in saying that you walked around Grubori with Mr. Turkalj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's too much background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
